newsitem.title: JAPAN: Shokochukin Bank says privatisation infeasible.
newsitem.headline: Shokochukin Bank says privatisation infeasible.

text.p: The privatisation of Shokochukin Bank is not pragmatic and would hinder the bank's efforts to provide low-cost loans to small companies, an official for the bank said on Friday.

"The purpose of the Shokochukin Bank is to provide...loans to small enterprises. We are concerned that privatisation will make it impossible for us to live up to our objectives," the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Reuters in an interview.
Privatisation may lead to a downgrade in the bank's credit rating and raise the cost of its fund raising, he said.
"Our ability to raise low-cost funds comes from our creditworthiness, which I think is due to the fact that the government has a stake (in the bank)," he said.
"I think privatisation would mean, for example, that the government's stake in our bank would have to be returned. I think that would be difficult in reality," the official added.

The government's stake in the bank was 298.5 billion yen as of end-March 1996 and accounted for 77.8 percent of its capital. The remainder of its capital, worth 85.3 billion yen, was provided by the private sector.
The Shokochukin Bank raises most of its funds by issuing bank debentures, which totalled 12.08 trillion yen outstanding as of end-March 1996.
Shokochukin's five-year bank debentures issued in April with a coupon rate of 1.6 percent were quoted at around 2.03 percent on Friday.
By contrast, the Industrial Bank of Japan's benchmark April five-year debentures with a coupon rate of 1.6 percent were traded at 1.93 percent on Friday.
Bond traders said the yields on Shokochukin Bank's debentures began rising in April, when a senior ruling party official said he was confident that the bank could be privatised.

"Before there was only a spread of about three basis points between IBJ and Shokochukin debentures, but now it has widened to anywhere from three to 10 basis points," said a trader for a trust bank's securities unit.

Shokochukin Bank, which had 11.5 trillion yen in loans outstanding as of the end of 1996, is one of the government-affiliated financial institutions being considered for possible reform by the ruling Liberal Democratic Party.
Shinji Sato, Japan's trade minister, said on April 15 that privatisation of Shokochukin Bank would be difficult to implement. The ministry is responsible for supervising the bank.
Sato said private banks were not particularly willing to take over the governments' nearly 300 billion yen stake.
The LDP's administrative reform panel is expected to unveil its reform plan for government-affiliated financial institutions later this month.
